title: Charge balance
prompt: Which formula represents aluminum sulfate?
explain: Two Al³⁺ ions and three SO₄²⁻ ions give total charge zero.
why: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ don’t balance one-to-one: +3 and −2 leave a +1 charge.
Three Al³⁺ (+9) and one SO₄²⁻ (−2) don’t balance.
The sulfate needs parentheses and a subscript: two Al³⁺ (+6) need three SO₄²⁻ (−6).

title: Cation electron configuration
prompt: What is the ground-state electron configuration of Fe2+?
explain: Fe loses its two 4s electrons before 3d electrons.
why: Right electron count, but ions lose their 4s electrons first.
Right electron count, but both 4s electrons leave before any 3d electron.
That has 26 electrons. Fe²⁺ has 24.

title: Ion vs atom
prompt: What happens when a neutral Mg atom becomes Mg2+?
explain: Ion formation changes electrons, not the nuclear proton count.
why: The nucleus doesn’t change when an ion forms; only electrons move.
Gaining electrons gives a negative ion. A 2+ charge means two electrons were lost.
Neutrons have no charge, so losing them can’t make an ion.

title: Periodic trends
prompt: Which atom is larger: Na or Cl, in the same period?
explain: Across a period, increasing effective nuclear charge generally contracts atomic radius.
why: Across a period, more protons pull the same shell in, so Cl is smaller.
Atoms in the same period differ in size: radius shrinks left to right.
Atomic radius has a clear trend: it decreases across a period.

title: Isoelectronic ions
prompt: Which is larger: O2− or Mg2+?
explain: Both have 10 electrons; lower nuclear charge gives O²⁻ the larger radius.
why: Both have 10 electrons, but Mg²⁺ has 12 protons pulling them in, so it is smaller.
Same electron count, different nuclear charge (8 vs 12), so different sizes.
Both ions still have 10 electrons.

title: Electronegativity
prompt: Which atom is most electronegative?
explain: Fluorine has the greatest electronegativity among these atoms.
why: Na is on the far left, so it is one of the least electronegative.
C is fairly electronegative, but F (top right) is the most electronegative element.
Mg is a metal on the left side, with low electronegativity.

title: Quantum numbers
prompt: Which quantum-number pair is impossible?
explain: For a given n, l ranges from 0 through n − 1.
why: Allowed: for n = 3, l can be 0, 1 or 2.
Allowed: for n = 2, l can be 0 or 1.
Allowed: for n = 1, l must be 0.

title: Hund’s rule
prompt: How are three electrons arranged in three degenerate p orbitals?
answer: One in each orbital, parallel spins
choices: One in each orbital, parallel spins
Pair two before filling the third
explain: Singly occupy each equal-energy orbital with parallel spins before pairing.
why: Hund’s rule: fill each equal-energy orbital singly before pairing.
One orbital holds at most two electrons (Pauli exclusion).
An orbital can hold only two electrons, with opposite spins.

title: Empirical vs molecular
prompt: A compound has empirical formula CH2O and molar mass 180.16 g/mol. Which molecular formula fits?
explain: The empirical formula mass is about 30.03 g/mol; multiplier ≈ 6.
why: CH₂O has a molar mass of only about 30 g/mol. 180.16 ÷ 30.03 ≈ 6.
That is about 90 g/mol, only half of 180.16.
That is about 360 g/mol, twice 180.16.

title: Sig figs
prompt: How many significant figures are in 0.004070?
explain: Leading zeros are placeholders; the internal zero and trailing decimal zero are significant.
why: The zero between 7 and the end counts, and so does the trailing zero after the decimal.
The trailing zero after a decimal point is significant too: 4, 0, 7, 0.
Leading zeros (0.00) are placeholders and never count.

title: Accuracy vs precision
prompt: Measurements cluster tightly but far from the accepted value. They are…
explain: Precision concerns agreement among measurements; accuracy concerns agreement with the accepted value.
why: Accurate means close to the accepted value, which these aren’t. Clustering tightly means precise.
They are far from the accepted value, so they aren’t accurate.
These are real measurements; they are just consistently off.

title: Matter classification
prompt: A uniform salt solution is best classified as…
choices: A heterogeneous mixture with visible phases
explain: A solution is a homogeneous mixture; its composition can vary.
why: Salt water contains more than one substance, so it is a mixture.
Its composition can vary (more or less salt), so it is a mixture, not a compound.
A solution looks the same throughout, so it is homogeneous.

title: Intermolecular forces
prompt: What strongest intermolecular attraction occurs between water molecules?
explain: Water has hydrogen bonded to oxygen and an oxygen lone pair on neighboring molecules.
why: O–H covalent bonds are inside each molecule. Between molecules, the attraction is hydrogen bonding.
Metallic bonding is in metals, not water.
Water has dispersion forces, but its strongest attraction is hydrogen bonding.

title: Dispersion forces
prompt: Which statement about London dispersion forces is correct?
answer: All atoms and molecules exhibit them
choices: All atoms and molecules exhibit them
They require hydrogen bonded to fluorine
explain: Temporary correlated electron-density fluctuations create dispersion attractions.
why: Every atom and molecule has dispersion forces, polar or not.
They are weak attractions between molecules, not bonds inside them.
That describes hydrogen bonding, not dispersion.

title: Vapor pressure
prompt: At the same temperature, stronger intermolecular attractions generally give…
explain: Fewer molecules escape into the vapor when attractions are stronger.
why: Stronger attractions hold molecules in the liquid, so fewer escape: vapor pressure goes down.
Some molecules always escape, so vapor pressure isn’t zero.
Stronger attractions raise the boiling point.

title: Dissolving a salt
prompt: What interaction helps stabilize ions in water?
choices: Only ion–ion attractions in a crystal
Covalent bonding of every ion to water
explain: Water’s polar dipoles hydrate dissolved ions.
why: Once dissolved, the ions are surrounded by water, not by each other.
Water attracts ions through its partial charges; it doesn’t form covalent bonds with them.
That describes metals, not ions in water.

title: Entropy intuition
prompt: A gas expands into a larger volume at the same temperature. Which direction is favored for the gas entropy?
explain: The gas has more accessible positional microstates in the larger volume.
why: More volume gives the particles more possible positions, so entropy increases.
Entropy depends on volume for a gas, so it changes.
Entropy is positive for any real substance; here it increases.

title: Dissolution energetics
prompt: Breaking an ionic lattice by separating its ions is…
explain: Separating oppositely charged ions requires energy; hydration releases energy. The total can have either sign.
why: Pulling opposite charges apart takes energy.
Neutralization is an acid–base reaction, not separating ions.
No electrons are gained when ions are separated.

title: Electrolytes
prompt: Which gives the greatest ideal dissolved-particle concentration at equal formula-equivalent molarity?
explain: Complete dissociation gives AlCl₃ four ions, CaCl₂ three, NaCl two; glucose stays molecular.
why: NaCl gives 2 ions per formula unit; AlCl₃ gives 4.
Glucose doesn’t dissociate, so it gives just 1 particle.
CaCl₂ gives 3 ions; AlCl₃ gives 4.

title: Kinetic molecular theory
prompt: Two ideal gases have the same temperature. They have the same…
explain: Average translational kinetic energy depends on absolute temperature; average speeds also depend on mass.
why: Lighter molecules move faster at the same temperature, so speeds differ.
Temperature says nothing about which gas it is.
Density depends on molar mass and pressure, not only temperature.

title: Crystal classes
prompt: Which solid is a covalent network?
explain: Diamond has an extended covalent network; molecular or atomic solids are held by intermolecular attractions.
why: Argon atoms are held by weak dispersion forces: an atomic solid.
NaCl is an ionic solid.
Methane molecules are held by dispersion forces: a molecular solid.

title: Colligative idea
prompt: Which changes depend primarily on dissolved-particle count in the ideal dilute limit?
choices: Chemical identity alone determines all effects
Atomic number of the solvent only
explain: Colligative properties depend on solute particle concentration, with electrolyte dissociation affecting particle count.
why: Colligative properties depend on how many particles there are, not what they are.
The solvent matters, but the change depends on the number of solute particles.
Oxidation states have nothing to do with colligative properties.

title: Strong acid in water
prompt: What best represents HCl(aq)?
explain: HCl ionizes essentially completely in water: HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻.
why: HCl is a strong acid, so it ionizes completely in water.
HCl gives ions (H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻), not neutral atoms.
(aq) means dissolved in water.

title: Weak acid in water
prompt: What best describes CH3COOH(aq) before adding base?
answer: Mostly acid molecules with some ions
choices: Mostly acid molecules with some ions
Only free H+ and acetate ions
explain: A weak acid is only partially ionized. Weak does not mean dilute.
why: Acetic acid is weak, so only a small fraction ionizes.
The acid molecules are dissolved in the water.
Acetic acid stays as molecules; it doesn’t break into atoms.

title: Weak acid + strong base
prompt: Choose the net ionic reaction.
explain: Do not split a weak acid into ions. Hydroxide removes its acidic proton and produces conjugate base.
why: NaCl is soluble, so it doesn’t precipitate. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectators.
Acids don’t break down into elements in water.
That is electrolysis, not an acid–base reaction.

title: At equivalence
prompt: A weak monoprotic acid is titrated exactly with NaOH. What acid-derived species dominates after stoichiometric reaction?
explain: Neutralization makes the conjugate base. Subsequent hydrolysis is an equilibrium problem, not extra stoichiometric OH⁻.
why: At equivalence, the added OH⁻ has used up the acid.
Exact titration means no extra OH⁻ was added.
Na⁺ stays as an ion; no metal atoms form.

title: Salt or precipitate?
prompt: NaNO3(aq) appears in a molecular precipitation equation. What is actually dissolved?
explain: Soluble strong electrolytes remain as hydrated ions.
why: NaNO₃ is ionic and soluble, so it exists as separate ions.
Dissolving doesn’t change ions into elements.
All nitrates are soluble, so NaNO₃ doesn’t precipitate.

title: Net ionic spectators
prompt: For HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq), which ions are spectators?
explain: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ remain dissolved before and after the reaction.
why: These react to make water, so they aren’t spectators.
OH⁻ reacts with H₃O⁺, so it isn’t a spectator.
H₃O⁺ reacts with OH⁻, so it isn’t a spectator.

title: Gas evolution
prompt: Acid reacts with carbonate. Which products explain the bubbling?
explain: Carbonic acid formed by protonating carbonate decomposes into CO₂ and water.
why: No oxygen is made. The gas is CO₂ from H₂CO₃ breaking down.
That would be splitting water; acid + carbonate gives CO₂.
The carbon leaves as CO₂ gas.

title: Equivalence vs endpoint
prompt: Which statement is correct?
answer: Equivalence is stoichiometric; endpoint is an observed signal
choices: Equivalence is stoichiometric; endpoint is an observed signal
They always mean exactly the same volume
explain: The endpoint is the indicator or instrument response; it approximates equivalence.
why: The endpoint is where the indicator changes; it only approximates equivalence.
Spectator ions remain at the endpoint.
Only strong acid + strong base gives pH 7 at equivalence; a weak acid gives a basic solution.

title: Water orientation
prompt: Which end of water points preferentially toward Ca2+?
explain: Oxygen is the partially negative end; ion–dipole attractions hydrate cations.
why: The H end is partly positive, so it is repelled by a cation.
Water is polar, so one end is attracted more.
Water is polar: O is δ− and H is δ+.

title: Precipitation
prompt: AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) forms AgCl(s). Which pair is removed into the solid?
explain: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s); Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ remain dissolved.
why: Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ stay dissolved: they are spectators.
NaCl is soluble; the solid is AgCl.
AgNO₃ is soluble; the solid is AgCl.

title: Equilibrium is dynamic
prompt: A reaction has reached equilibrium. What is true?
answer: The forward and reverse rates are equal
choices: The forward and reverse rates are equal
Reactant and product concentrations must be equal
All reactants have been used up
explain: At equilibrium both reactions continue at the same rate, so concentrations stay constant (not necessarily equal).
why: Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions keep going, at equal rates.
Concentrations are constant, not necessarily equal.
At equilibrium reactants and products are both present.

title: Square brackets
prompt: In kinetics and equilibrium, what does [NO2] mean?
choices: The mass of NO2 in grams
The partial pressure of NO2 in torr
explain: Brackets mean molarity: moles of solute per liter of solution or container volume.
why: Square brackets mean concentration in mol/L, not mass.
Brackets mean molarity, not a count of molecules.
Partial pressure is written P(NO₂). Brackets mean mol/L.

title: Phases in an equation
prompt: In CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g), which species is a gas?
explain: Read the state symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water. Only CO₂ is (g).
why: CaCO₃ is marked (s): solid.
CaO is marked (s): solid.
CO₂ is marked (g).

title: Heat in an equation
prompt: For N2(g) + 3 H2(g) → 2 NH3(g), ΔH = −92 kJ. Where does heat appear if you write it into the equation?
explain: A negative ΔH (exothermic) releases heat, so heat is written on the product side.
why: A negative ΔH means heat is released, so heat is a product.
Heat appears on one side only: products for exothermic.
ΔH = −92 kJ means heat is released.

title: Endothermic
prompt: ΔH = +57 kJ for N2O4(g) → 2 NO2(g). What does this mean?
answer: The reaction absorbs heat; heat acts like a reactant
choices: The reaction absorbs heat; heat acts like a reactant
The reaction releases heat; heat acts like a product
explain: Positive ΔH is endothermic: heat is taken in, so it behaves like a reactant.
why: A positive ΔH means heat is absorbed, not released.
ΔH says nothing about speed.
Endothermic reactions happen all the time; they just take in heat.

title: Catalyst
prompt: What does a catalyst do?
answer: Speeds up a reaction without being used up
choices: Speeds up a reaction without being used up
Is used up as a reactant
explain: A catalyst gives a faster pathway (lower activation energy) and is regenerated; ΔH and products are unchanged.
why: A catalyst speeds up the same reaction; the products are unchanged.
A catalyst is regenerated at the end.
A catalyst doesn’t change ΔH.

title: Why reactions speed up
prompt: Why does raising the temperature usually speed up a reaction?
answer: Particles move faster and collide harder and more often
choices: Particles move faster and collide harder and more often
The number of reactant molecules increases
explain: Faster particles collide more often and more of the collisions have enough energy to react.
why: Temperature doesn’t change molecular size.
Heating doesn’t create molecules; it makes them move faster.
Products form faster, not slower.

title: Strong or weak acid
prompt: Which acid is weak (only partly ionized in water)?
explain: On the green sheet, HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄ and HClO₄ are strong; HF is weak.
why: HCl is one of the strong acids on the green sheet.
HNO₃ is one of the strong acids on the green sheet.
HBr is one of the strong acids on the green sheet.

title: Concentration and collisions
prompt: You double the concentration of a reactant in solution. What happens to the collisions per second?
answer: They increase (more particles in the same volume)
choices: They increase (more particles in the same volume)
explain: More particles per liter means more frequent collisions, a key idea behind rate laws.
why: More particles in the same space collide more often, not less.
More particles per liter means more collisions.
Adding reactant can’t stop collisions.

title: Gas pressure and moles
prompt: At constant T and V, you double the moles of a gas. What happens to its pressure?
explain: P = nRT/V, so at constant T and V pressure is directly proportional to moles.
why: P = nRT/V: pressure goes up with moles, not down.
More particles hit the walls, so pressure rises.
More gas means more pressure.

title: Which log?
prompt: pH = −log[H⁺]. Which calculator key?
explain: pH and pOH use base 10. Rate laws, Arrhenius and ΔG = −RT ln K use ln.
why: ln is base e. pH uses base-10 log.
eˣ undoes ln; it doesn’t take a log.
Squaring isn’t a log.

title: Undoing ln
prompt: You know ln K = 3.2. Which key gives K?
explain: ln is undone by e to the power: K = e³·².
why: 10ˣ undoes log (base 10). ln is undone by eˣ.
Squaring doesn’t undo a log.
The reciprocal doesn’t undo a log.

title: Negative logs
prompt: The log of a concentration like 2 × 10⁻⁵ M is…
explain: Numbers between 0 and 1 have negative logs. −log makes pH positive.
why: Numbers less than 1 have negative logs. −log gives +4.7, which is the pH-style value.
log 1 = 0; this number is much smaller than 1.
Log is undefined only for zero or negative numbers.

title: Straight-line test
prompt: You want k from a first-order reaction. Which plot is a straight line with slope −k?
explain: ln[A] = −kt + ln[A]₀ has the form y = mx + b. (Zero order: [A] vs t; second order: 1/[A] vs t.)
why: That is straight for zero order, with slope −k there.
That is straight for second order, with slope +k.
No common rate law gives a straight line for [A]².

title: Slope units
prompt: On a plot of [A] (M) against time (s), the slope has units of…
explain: Slope = Δy ÷ Δx, so y-units over x-units.
why: Slope is y-units over x-units: M over s.
Slope divides by the x-axis units (s).
Slope carries y-units over x-units.

title: Which root?
prompt: A quadratic from an ICE table gives x = 0.031 and x = −0.52. Which is right?
answer: x = 0.031 (a concentration change can’t be negative)
choices: x = 0.031 (a concentration change can’t be negative)
explain: Pick the root that keeps every concentration positive.
why: A negative x would make a concentration negative here.
Only one root keeps every concentration positive.
x = 0.031 works: all concentrations stay positive.

title: Exponent rule
prompt: (3.0 × 10⁻⁴)² equals…
explain: Square the number and double the exponent: 3.0² = 9.0 and (10⁻⁴)² = 10⁻⁸.
why: Squaring doubles the exponent: (10⁻⁴)² = 10⁻⁸, not 10⁻¹⁶.
Square the 3.0 too: 3.0² = 9.0.

title: Doubling test
prompt: Rate = k[A]². If [A] is doubled, the rate…
explain: Second order in A: rate scales with the square of the change.
why: Second order: rate goes with [A]², so doubling [A] gives 2² = 4 times.
The rate depends on [A], so it changes.
Raising [A] raises the rate.

title: kJ with ln
prompt: ΔG° = −RT ln K with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). ΔG° is given in kJ/mol. What first?
choices: Convert R to kJ by dividing by 10
explain: R is in joules, so ΔG° must be in joules too. (Converting R to kJ by ÷1000 also works.)
why: J to kJ is ÷1000, not ÷10.
R is in J and ΔG° in kJ, so they don’t match yet.
Thermodynamics always uses kelvins.

title: 5% rule
prompt: You used x ≈ √(Kc) and found x is 2% of c. Is the shortcut OK?
explain: Under 5% means c − x ≈ c was a fine approximation.
why: The usual cutoff is 5%.
x can’t be zero if the reaction happens at all.
The test is the 5% check, not K > 1; small K is when the shortcut works.
